modern_osis:
Numbers — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

This book is called Numbers because it records several censuses of the people of Israel.

Its account extends from the giving of the law at Sinai until Israel reached the plains beside the Jordan River.

It tells how the people complained and refused to believe, and how they were therefore sentenced to wander in the wilderness for nearly forty years.

The book also contains laws, some moral and others ceremonial.

The people's trials helped reveal the difference between wicked people and hypocrites, on the one hand, and God's true and faithful servants, who worshiped him sincerely, on the other.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe numbering of the Israelites.1–43The number of the people.44–46The Levites not numbered with the rest.47–54
Israel's tribes are counted (verses 1–43)

God commanded a census of Israel.

The count showed his faithfulness in causing Jacob's descendants to increase so greatly.

It also helped organize the people for the coming wars and conquest of Canaan and established their family divisions for the future distribution of land.

The census counted, from each tribe, those able to serve in war.

Israel had not yet encountered these enemies, but battles awaited them.

Christians should likewise prepare to withstand the enemies of their souls, even when everything appears peaceful.

The total number of Israelites (verses 44–46)

The census gave a large total.

Consider how much food was needed to maintain such a crowd in the wilderness!

God supplied everyone's needs day by day.

When we recognize his faithfulness in fulfilling promises that once seemed impossible, we can take courage concerning the promises still awaiting fulfillment for his church.

The Levites are counted separately (verses 47–54)

The tribe of Levi was set apart.

Its members had distinguished themselves during the crisis of the golden calf.

Those who perform extraordinary service for God may receive extraordinary honors from him.

The Levites were entrusted with the tabernacle and its sacred treasures, both when Israel was camped and when it moved.

It honored the holy things that only those called by God could see or handle them.

None of us is naturally fit or worthy to enjoy fellowship with God.

We must first be called by grace into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

As the spiritual offspring of our great High Priest, Christians are made priests to God.

We should be especially careful to prevent sin, because preventing sin is also preventing the judgment it brings.

As a holy tribe, the Levites were not numbered with the other Israelites.

Those who minister in holy things should not allow worldly concerns to entangle them or become entangled themselves in worldly affairs.

Every believer should seek to do what the Lord has commanded.

[Num.1.1-Num.1.43]
Numbers
This book is called NUMBERS from the several numberings of the people contained in it. It extends from the giving of the law at Sinai, till their arrival in the plains of Jordan. An account is given of their murmuring and unbelief, for which they were sentenced to wander in the wilderness nearly forty years; also some laws, both, moral and ceremonial. Their trials greatly tended to distinguish the wicked and hypocrites from the faithful and true servants of God, who served him with a pure heart.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The numbering of the Israelites. | (1-43) |
The number of the people. | (44-46) |
The Levites not numbered with the rest. | (47-54) |
Verses 1-43
The people were numbered to show God's faithfulness in thus increasing the seed of Jacob, that they might be the better trained for the wars and conquest of Canaan, and to ascertain their families in order to the division of the land. It is said of each tribe, that those were numbered who were able to go forth to war; they had wars before them, though now they met with no opposition. Let the believer be prepared to withstand the enemies of his soul, though all may appear to be peace.
[Num.1.44-Num.1.46]
Verses 44-46
We have here the sum total. How much was required to maintain all these in the wilderness! They were all provided for by God every day. When we observe the faithfulness of God, however unlikely the performance of his promise may appear, we may take courage as to those which yet remain to be fulfilled to the church of God.
[Num.1.47-Num.1.54]
Verses 47-54
Care is here taken to distinguish the tribe of Levi, which, in the matter of the golden calf, had distinguished itself. Singular services shall be recompensed by singular honours. It was to the honour of the Levites, that to them was committed the care of the tabernacle and its treasures, in their camps and in their marches. It was for the honour of the holy things that none should see them, or touch them, but those who were called of God to the service. We all are unfit and unworthy to have fellowship with God, till called by his grace into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and so, being the spiritual seed of that great High Priest, we are made priests to our God. Great care must be taken to prevent sin, for preventing sin is preventing wrath. Being a holy tribe, they were not reckoned among other Israelites. They that minister about holy things, should neither entangle themselves, nor be entangled, in worldly affairs. And let every believer seek to do what the Lord has commanded.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The order of the tribes in their tents.

The arrangement of Israel's camp

The tribes camped around the tabernacle, which stood in the middle of Israel's camp.

The tabernacle showed God's gracious presence among his people.

Yet the people had to place their tents at a respectful distance from the sanctuary.

The Israelites took their assigned positions without complaining or arguing.

Their orderly camp was both safer and more beautiful because of this obedience.

It is both our duty and our advantage to be satisfied with the position God has given us.

We should carry out our responsibilities well without envy, resentment, ambition or greed.

The church of the gospel should likewise be well joined together according to Scripture's pattern.

Each member should know and keep the appropriate place within the body.

When this happens, everyone who loves the church can rejoice at its good order (Colossians 2:5).

The order of the tribes in their tents.
--The tribes were to encamp about the tabernacle, which was to be in the midst of them. It was a token of God's gracious presence. Yet they were to pitch their tents afar off, in reverence to the sanctuary. The children of Israel put themselves in their posts, without murmuring or disputing; and as it was their safety, so it was their beauty. It is our duty and interest to be contented with the place allotted to us, and to endeavour to occupy it in a proper manner, without envying or murmuring; without ambition or covetousness. Thus the gospel church ought to be compact, according to the Scripture model, every one knowing and keeping his place; and then all that wish well to the church rejoice, beholding their order, [Col.2.5] Col 2:5.

The Levites replace Israel's firstborn (verses 1–13)

Aaron and his two sons had a great deal of priestly work to carry out.

God appointed the Levites to help them.

Whenever he provides work for his servants, he can also provide the help they need.

The Levites were taken in place of Israel's firstborn.

When God saves us—as he saved Israel's firstborn—we receive an additional obligation to serve him faithfully.

The right God has over us through redemption confirms the right he already possesses as our Creator.

The families and duties of Levi (verses 14–39)

The Levites were grouped according to Levi's three sons: Gershon, Kohath and Merari.

Each group was further divided into families.

Moses' descendants received no special rank or privilege above the other Levites.

This showed that Moses was not using his position to advance his own household or obtain special honors for his family.

Levi was by far the smallest of Israel's tribes.

God's chosen people are likewise a small flock compared with the world.

The number of the firstborn and their ransom (verses 40–51)

The number of Israel's firstborn came close to the number of Levites.

God knows all his works before they happen.

The numbers were arranged in an exact relationship, which became clear when they were compared.

The small number of firstborn who exceeded the number of Levites were to be redeemed by a payment given to Aaron.

The church is called the church of the firstborn.

But it is not redeemed with silver or gold.

Because our sins have placed us under God's just judgment, only the precious blood of his Son can ransom us.

Every human being belongs to the Lord by creation.

Every true Christian belongs to him also by redemption.

We should each know our own responsibility.

No service required by such a Master should be dismissed as beneath us or too difficult.

Levites in their prime serve the sanctuary (verses 1–3)

Levites aged thirty to fifty were appointed for the main service of the tabernacle.

Serving God deserves the best of our strength and the finest part of our lives.

Our time cannot be better spent than honoring him who is first and best.

We should take up God's work while we are most energetic and capable.

Those who postpone repentance until old age have failed to understand this.

They leave the most important work to the least favorable time.

The duties of Kohath's descendants (verses 4–20)

The Kohathites carried the tabernacle's most holy furnishings.

The sacred objects had to be covered, both to protect them and to treat them with reverence.

They were also kept from ordinary sight.

The covering pictured the mystery surrounding the spiritual truths represented by the sanctuary, and the limited light given under that earlier religious order.

Through Christ, our situation has changed.

We are now encouraged to approach the throne of grace boldly.

The duties of Gershon and Merari (verses 21–33)

The other two Levite families were assigned work that seemed less honorable than Kohath's responsibilities.

Yet their duties were just as necessary and had to be carried out carefully.

Each object was assigned to their care by name.

This illustrated God's concern for his church and for every individual member.

Scripture compares the death of believers to dismantling a tent (2 Corinthians 5:1) or taking it off (2 Peter 1:14).

But our bodies will be raised on the great day.

They will be transformed to resemble Christ's glorious body, and we will remain with him forever.

The number of Levites fit for service (verses 34–49)

God arranged the numbers in a surprising way.

Although the Merarites were the smallest family group, they had the greatest number of men capable of service.

God equips people for whatever work he assigns them.

He supplies strength suited to the task and sufficient grace to perform it.

Even the least numerous of Israel's other tribes had more able men than the Levites.

Similarly, more people devote themselves to the business of this world than to God's service.

May our souls be wholly given to serving him.

Cleansing the camp and making restitution (verses 1–10)

Israel's camp had to be kept clean.

The church's purity deserves just as much attention as its peace and order.

Those who were ceremonially defiled had to be separated from the camp.

Wisdom from above is pure first, and then peaceable.

The more openly a home or family professes faith, the more carefully it should put away wickedness.

When one person cheats or exploits another, the offense is also committed against the Lord, who commands us to act justly.

What should someone do when an awakened conscience recalls dishonesty committed many years earlier?

The person must confess the sin both to God and to the neighbor who was harmed.

This can be humiliating, especially if it requires admitting a past lie. But it remains necessary.

Both the wrong against God and the financial loss suffered by the neighbor must be addressed.

Restitution alone is not enough without genuine faith and repentance.

And as long as someone knowingly keeps what was obtained through injustice, the guilt remains.

Neither religious sacrifices, prayers nor tears can erase an offense that the sinner is deliberately continuing to commit.

This principle is taught both by sound reasoning and by God's word.

It exposes hypocrisy, while guiding a tender conscience toward faithful action and the inward peace that comes through faith in Christ.

The trial of jealousy (verses 11–31)

This law encouraged Israelite wives to avoid conduct that gave reasonable grounds for suspicion.

It also restrained husbands from acting cruelly because of suspicion alone.

The guilty were not to escape judgment, and innocent wives were not to be condemned unjustly.

When there was no evidence sufficient to decide the case, the woman was called to appeal solemnly to the God who knows every heart.

If she was guilty, she could not sincerely accept the oath and drink the prescribed water unless she refused to believe God or defiantly disregarded his justice.

The water was called bitter because it brought a curse upon the guilty.

Sin, too, is bitter.

Anyone who pursues forbidden pleasures should remember the misery that follows them.

Henry draws three lessons.

First, God knows every secret sin.

He sometimes exposes hidden wrongdoing even during this life.

A final day is coming when God will judge human secrets through Jesus Christ (Romans 2:16).

Second, God will judge sexual immorality and adultery.

We no longer have this ordeal involving bitter water, but we have God's word, which should warn us no less seriously.

Sinful lust ends in bitterness.

Third, God will make the innocence of the innocent known.

The same act of providence can help some people while harming others, according to God's righteous purposes.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe law concerning the Nazarites.1–21The form of blessing the people.22–27
The Nazirite vow (verses 1–21)

The word Nazirite means someone set apart.

Some people, including Samson and John the Baptist, were appointed by God before their birth for lifelong consecration.

Ordinarily, however, a Nazirite vow was taken voluntarily for a limited period.

It involved separation from ordinary worldly pleasures and special dedication to God's service.

Scripture already mentions Nazirites as a known class, but this chapter gives definite rules for their obligations.

God supplied those rules so that superstition would not endlessly add further restrictions.

Nazirites were forbidden wine, strong drink and even grapes.

Those who dedicate themselves to God must not let physical appetite rule them.

Christians should practice moderation in alcoholic drinks; once someone becomes ruled by them, Satan finds that person easier to trap.

Nazirites were to avoid everything produced by the vine.

This teaches us to keep away not only from sin itself but also from things near it that draw us into temptation.

They were forbidden to cut their hair or shave during the vow.

This marked their willingness to forgo bodily ease and outward adornment.

It was also the outward sign of Samson's lifelong separation.

They must not touch ritually unclean things.

Likewise, people devoted to God should keep their consciences pure from dead works.

Through every day of the vow they were to be holy to the Lord.

Without inward holiness, all their outward abstinence was worthless.

For deliberate, defiant violation of the vow, Henry notes that no specific penalty or sacrifice was appointed: the guilty would have to answer to God.

But the law made provision for those whose vows were disrupted without willful sin.

Henry contrasts these vows with the religious orders of the Roman Catholic Church as he understood them.

He argues that the rules are fundamentally different, not that Nazirites directly authorize those later orders.

Unlike those orders, Nazirites were not forbidden marriage, nor were they subject to a general ban on permitted foods.

They abstained completely from wine, whereas the orders Henry criticizes did not.

Ordinary Nazirites chose a temporary period rather than making a lifelong vow, and in certain circumstances a parent or husband had authority concerning the vow.

This is Henry's historical and confessional criticism; it should not be treated as an editorial claim independently established for the modern world.

Christ is not only our Surety, but also our example.

For his sake we should renounce sinful pleasures, resist fleshly desires, separate ourselves from sin, openly confess our faith, moderate our natural affections, cultivate spiritual thinking and devote ourselves to God's service.

Our lives should encourage others to follow him.

The priestly blessing (verses 22–27)

The priests were appointed to bless the people solemnly in the Lord's name.

What makes up this blessing?

God's almighty protection as our Savior.

His favor, like the smile of a loving Father or the warmth of sunlight.

His forgiveness of sins, provision for our needs, comfort in sorrow and grace preparing us for eternal glory.

Together these are the greatest blessings anyone can receive.

Compared with them, worldly pleasures scarcely deserve mention.

This blessing was also a form of prayer.

The name Jehovah appears three times.

Henry notes that Jewish interpreters saw a mystery in the repetition.

He believes the New Testament explains it: we are to look for grace from the Lord Jesus Christ, love from God the Father and fellowship from the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:14).

Each Person is Jehovah, yet there are not three Lords but one Lord.

Verses 1-21
The word Nazarite signifies separation. Some were appointed of God, before their birth, to be Nazarites all their days, as Samson and John the Baptist. But, in general, it was a vow of separation from the world and devotedness to the services of religion, for a limited time, and under certain rules, which any person might make if they pleased. A Nazarite is spoken of as well known; but his obligation is brought to a greater certainty than before. That the fancies of superstitious men might not multiply the restraints endlessly, God gives them rules. They must not drink wine or strong drink, nor eat grapes. Those who separate themselves to God, must not gratify the desires of the body, but keep it under. Let all Christians be very moderate in the use of wine and strong drink; for if the love of these once gets the mastery of a man, he becomes an easy prey to Satan. The Nazarites were to eat nothing that came of the vine; this may teach the utmost care to avoid sin, and all that borders upon it, and leads to it, or may be a temptation to us. They must not cut their hair. They must neither poll their heads, nor shave their beards; this was the mark of Samson being a Nazarite. This signified neglect of the body, and of the ease and ornament of it. Those who separate themselves to God, must keep their consciences pure from dead works, and not touch unclean things. All the days of their separation they must be holy to the Lord. This was the meaning of those outward observances, and without this they were of no account. No penalty or sacrifice was appointed for those who wilfully broke their vow of being Nazarites; they must answer another day for such profane trifling with the Lord their God; but those were to be relieved who did not sin wilfully. There is nothing in Scripture that bears the least resemblance to the religious orders of the church of Rome, except these Nazarites. But mark the difference, or rather how completely opposed! The religious of that church are forbidden to marry; but no such restriction is laid upon the Nazarites. They are commanded to abstain from meats; but the Nazarites might eat any food allowed other Israelites. They are not generally forbidden wine, not even on their fasting days; but the Nazarites might not have wine at any time. Their vow is lasting, even to the end of their lives; the Nazarites' vow was only for a limited time, at their own will; and in certain cases not unless allowed by husbands or parents. Such a thorough difference there is between rules of man's invention and those directed in Scripture, Let us not forget that the Lord Jesus is not only our Surety, but also our example. For his sake we must renounce worldly pleasures, abstain from fleshy lusts, be separate from sinners, make open profession of our faith, moderate natural affections, be spiritually-minded, and devoted to God's service, and desirous to be an example all around us. ( [Num.6.22-Num.6.27] Nu 6:22-27)
[Num.6.22-Num.6.27]
Verses 22-27
The priests were solemnly to bless the people in the name of the Lord. To be under the almighty protection of God our Saviour; to enjoy his favour as the smile of a loving Father, or as the cheering beams of the sun; while he mercifully forgives our sins, supplies our wants, consoles the heart, and prepares us by his grace for eternal glory; these things form the substance of this blessing, and the sum total of all blessings. In so rich a list of mercies worldly joys are not worthy to be mentioned. Here is a form of prayer. The name Jehovah is three times repeated. The Jews think there is some mystery; and we know what it is, the New Testament having explained it. There we are directed to expect the blessing from the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of the Father, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, [2Cor.13.14] 2Co 13:14; each of which Persons is Jehovah, and yet they are not three Lords, but one Lord.

The leaders' offerings for the tabernacle (verses 1–9)

The tribal leaders brought their offerings for the tabernacle's service after the sanctuary had been fully erected.

Required acts of worship must take priority over voluntary gifts.

The more authority and resources God grants someone, the greater the opportunity to serve him and the surrounding community.

No sooner had the tabernacle been established than the people made provision for moving it.

Even when life seems newly settled, we should prepare for future changes and especially for death—the greatest change.

The leaders' offerings for the altar (verses 10–89)

The leaders and prominent men were among the first to take part in honoring God.

People in authority should use their position, influence and wealth to promote faith and God's service wherever they live.

This was a joyful festival of dedication.

Yet a sin offering appeared among the sacrifices.

Even when we serve God at our best, we remain aware of sin and need repentance.

In every act of worship, faith must look toward Christ as our Sin Offering.

Each leader brought an offering on a different day.

God's work should not be carried out in a confused rush.

Taking time may not make us finish faster, but it will help us do it better.

A task extending across twelve days should not be treated as a tedious burden.

The offerings were identical.

This showed that every tribe had an equal share in the altar and an equal right to the blessings signified by its sacrifices.

The One who spoke to Moses from between the cherubim—the Shekinah, or visible divine majesty—was, Henry says, the eternal Word, the second Person of the Trinity.

All God's fellowship with human beings comes through his Son.

Through that Son he created the world and rules the church.

He is the same yesterday, today and forever.

Aaron himself lit the sanctuary lamps.

Scripture shines like a light in a dark place (2 Peter 1:19).

Without that light, even the church would remain in darkness—just as the tabernacle, which had no windows, would have been dark without its lamps.

Ministers serve by lighting these lamps spiritually, explaining and applying God's word.

Jesus Christ is the only Light of our dark and sinful world.

Through his atoning work, his word and the Holy Spirit, he spreads his light.

These verses provide directions for solemnly setting apart the Levites.

All Israel needed to know that the Levites had not claimed this honor for themselves.

They were called to it by God.

But merely being set apart from others was not enough.

Those appointed for God's work must devote themselves to him and to the responsibilities he has assigned them.

Christians are to be baptized, and ministers are to be ordained.

Before offering God our work, we must offer him ourselves.

The Levites were to be cleansed.

Those who carry the Lord's vessels must be clean.

Moses sprinkled the appointed purifying water over them.

God declared his acceptance of the Levites.

Anyone who expects to enjoy the privileges of God's sanctuary should also be willing to perform its service.

On one hand, God does not need any of his creatures to serve him.

On the other, he never appoints anyone merely to carry a title while doing nothing.

Everyone he acknowledges as a servant receives work to do.

Even angels serve him.

The Passover and those unable to attend (verses 1–14)

God gave special instructions for observing this Passover.

So far as the record shows, Israel did not celebrate another Passover until arriving in Canaan (Joshua 5:10).

Henry sees this as early evidence that the ceremonial arrangements were not meant to last forever: some were allowed to fall into disuse for many years soon after they were established.

The Lord's Supper, by contrast, was not set aside during the church's earliest years, even though Christians then faced greater persecution and trouble than Israel had experienced in the wilderness.

Indeed, Henry says it was celebrated more frequently during the times of persecution than afterward.

Israel could hardly forget the Exodus while still living in the wilderness.

There was greater risk of forgetting it after settling in Canaan.

These verses also explain what should happen when people were ceremonially unclean at Passover.

Those whose hearts and consciences are polluted by sin cannot truly enjoy communion with God or the Christian Passover until they are cleansed through repentance and faith.

Notice how troubled the Israelites were when they were prevented from taking part in the Lord's offering.

We, too, should feel real sorrow when circumstances keep us from Sabbath worship or the Lord's Supper.

Moses did not decide the difficult case according to his own preference or feelings.

He waited for God's instruction.

Ministers must take their guidance from God's word.

When a case remains difficult, believers should take time to bring it before God in humble, trusting prayer, seeking the Spirit's direction.

God then gave a rule for this case and similar ones.

People who are unwillingly prevented from joining in God's ordinances may still expect his grace and favor amid their difficulties.

But people who deliberately refuse to participate should not presume upon his kindness.

God will not be mocked.

Israel moves when the cloud moves (verses 15–23)

The cloud was the visible sign of God's presence among Israel.

It taught the people that he remained near them day and night.

As long as the cloud rested above the tabernacle, they stayed in the same place.

Waiting for God's appointed time is never wasted time.

When the cloud rose, they traveled, even if the camp had been comfortable.

We do not know when we will leave the earthly tent of our bodies.

We should therefore remain prepared to move whenever the Lord calls us.

It is safe and good to go where God leads us and rest where he commands us to rest.

The cloud pictured the Holy Spirit's guidance.

We should not now expect the same visible signs of divine presence.

Yet God promises to direct his spiritual Israel by his counsel (Psalm 73:24), to guide them even to death (Psalm 48:14), and to lead all his children by his Spirit (Romans 8:14).

He makes straight the paths of people who acknowledge him in all their ways (Proverbs 3:6).

At every change of circumstance we should be willing to move or remain according to his command.

Our prayer should be, “Father, your will be done. Direct me and everything entrusted to me as you please. Only let me remain yours and follow my duty.”

Applying general biblical instructions to specific situations requires wise counsel and earnest prayer.

We must not confuse our own desires with divine guidance.

When something is obviously wrong—or even doubtful, and yet we strongly desire to do it—what someone calls “the cloud moving” may really be a temptation permitted by Satan.

People can imagine they are following God while actually following stubborn impulses.

The record of God's mercy and the truth of his word lead us reliably through Christ toward eternal peace.

Follow the pillar of cloud and fire: take the Bible to heart and humbly receive the word that can save your soul.

Those whose minds and consciences are defiled by sin, are unfit for communion with God, and cannot partake with comfort of the gospel passover, till they are cleansed by true repentance and faith. Observe with what trouble and concern these men complained that they were kept back from offering to the Lord. God gave directions in this case, and in other similar cases, explanatory of the law of the passover. As those who, against their minds, are forced to absent themselves from God's ordinances, may expect the favours of God's grace under their affliction, so those who, of choice, absent themselves, may expect God's wrath for their sin. Be not deceived: God is not mocked.

This cloud was appointed to be the visible sign and symbol of God's presence with Israel. Thus we are taught to see God always near us, both night and day. As long as the cloud rested on the tabernacle, so long they continued in the same place. There is no time lost, while we are waiting God's time. When the cloud was taken up, they removed, however comfortably they were encamped. The record of his mercy will conduct us with unerring truth, through Christ, to everlasting peace. Follow the pillar of the cloud and of fire. Lay the BIBLE to heart, and receive with meekness the ingrafted word, which is able to save your souls.

The silver trumpets (verses 1–10)

These verses establish the trumpet signals used to communicate publicly with the camp.

Israel was to receive its laws from God in every detail, so even these signals were given to Moses by divine command.

The trumpets pictured the preaching of the gospel.

It sounds an alarm to sinners, calling them to repent.

It announces freedom to people enslaved to Satan and gathers God's worshipers.

It directs and strengthens them on the journey to heaven.

It calls them to fight against the world and sin, and gives them confidence of victory.

It points them to Christ's sacrifice and reminds them of the Lord's presence protecting his people.

The gospel trumpet must make a clear and distinct sound.

Its message must suit both the people addressed and the purpose for speaking: conviction, humbling, comfort, encouragement, correction or instruction.

God has appointed the public proclamation of the gospel, and everyone to whom it comes is called to listen.

Israel travels from Sinai to Paran (verses 11–28)

The Israelites had spent nearly a year at Mount Sinai.

Now that their worship had been organized, they set out toward Canaan.

True religion begins with knowing God's holy law and humbling ourselves over sin.

But we must keep growing in the knowledge of Christ and his gospel, and in the powerful reasons, encouragements and help he gives us for holiness.

The people traveled when God commanded them (Deuteronomy 1:6–8) and when the cloud led them.

Those who submit to God's word and Spirit can follow a steady course even when the route seems confusing.

If we are sure that we have not lost our God and Guide, we need not fear becoming lost ourselves.

They left the wilderness of Sinai and camped in the wilderness of Paran.

So many of our changes in this world simply move us from one wilderness to another.

Moves that we expect to improve our circumstances do not always do so.

We will not find perfect rest or a permanent home until we reach heaven.

But everything will be well there.

Moses invites Hobab to accompany Israel (verses 29–32)

Moses invited his relative Hobab to come with the people to Canaan.

Those traveling toward the heavenly Canaan should invite and encourage friends to come too.

Other people sharing the joys of heaven will not reduce our own happiness in the least.

It is good to enjoy fellowship with people who enjoy fellowship with God.

Yet the visible attractions of this world can powerfully distract people from the unseen blessings of eternity.

Moses explained that Hobab could be useful to Israel.

He did not need Hobab to decide where to travel or camp—the cloud provided that guidance.

But Hobab could help identify practical features of the places they passed through or stayed in.

Depending on God's providence is entirely consistent with accepting wise help from our friends.

Moses prays when Israel moves and rests (verses 33–36)

Israel's departures and arrivals teach us to begin and end our daily journeys and work with prayer.

When the ark moved, Moses prayed for God to rise and scatter his enemies.

There are people who openly or secretly oppose God, his truth, laws, worship and people.

But God's rising to act is sufficient to defeat them.

When the ark rested, Moses prayed for the Lord to return and dwell with his people.

Israel's well-being and happiness depended on God's continuing presence.

Its safety did not come from its numbers but from his favor and his willingness to remain among the people.

God would go ahead and provide suitable places to rest during their travels.

He promised never to abandon or forsake them.

Here are directions concerning the public notices to be given the people by sound of trumpet. Their laws in every case were to be Divine, therefore, even in this matter Moses is directed. These trumpets typify the preached gospel. It sounds an alarm to sinners, calls them to repent, proclaims liberty to the captives and slaves of Satan, and collects the worshippers of God. It directs and encourages their heavenly journey; stirs them up to combat against the world and sin, encouraging them with the assurance of victory. It leads their attention to the sacrifice of Christ, and shows the Lord's presence for their protection. It is also necessary that the gospel trumpet give a distinct sound, according to the persons addressed, or the end proposed; whether to convince, humble, console, exhort, reprove, or teach. The sounding of the trumpet of the gospel is God's ordinance, and demands the attention of all to whom it is sent. ( [Num.10.11-Num.10.28] Nu 10:11-28)

After the Israelites had continued nearly a year at mount Sinai, and all was settled respecting their future worship, they began their march to Canaan. True religion begins with the knowledge of the holy law of God, and humiliation for sin, but we must go on towards perfection, in acquaintance with Christ and his gospel, and those effectual encouragements, motives, and assistances to holiness, which it proposes. They took their journey according to the commandment of the Lord, [Deut.1.6-Deut.1.8] De 1:6-8, and as the cloud led them. Those who give themselves to the direction of God's word and Spirit, steer a steady course, even when they seem bewildered. While they are sure they cannot lose their God and Guide, they need not fear losing their way. They went out of the wilderness of Sinai, and rested in the wilderness of Paran. All our removes in this world are but from one wilderness to another. The changes we think will be for the better do not always prove so. We shall never be at rest, never at home, till we come to heaven, but all will be well there.

Verses 29-32
Moses invites his kindred to go to Canaan. Those that are bound for the heavenly Canaan, should ask and encourage their friends to go with them: we shall have none the less of the joys of heaven, for others coming to share with us. It is good having fellowship with those who have fellowship with God. But the things of this world, which are seen, draw strongly from the pursuit of the things of the other world, which are not seen. Moses urges that Hobab might be serviceable to them. Not to show where they must encamp, nor what way they must march, the cloud was to direct that; but to show the conveniences of the place they marched through, and encamped in. It well consists with our trust in God's providence, to use the help of our friends.

Verses 33-36
Their going out and coming in, gives an example to us to begin and end every day's journey and every day's work with prayer. Here is Moses's prayer when the ark set forward, "Rise up, and let thine enemies be scattered." There are those in the world who are enemies to God and haters of him; secret and open enemies; enemies to his truths, his laws, his ordinances, his people. But for the scattering and defeating of God's enemies, there needs no more than God's arising. Observe also the prayer of Moses when the ark rested, that God would cause his people to rest. The welfare and happiness of the Israel of God, consist in the continual presence of God among them. Their safety is not in their numbers, but in the favour of God, and his gracious return to them, and resting with them. Upon this account, Happy art thou, O Israel! who is like unto thee, O people! God will go before them, to find them resting-places by the way. His promise is, and their prayers are, that he will never leave them nor forsake them.
